prompt: Gases were among the first substances studied using the modern scientific method. What did scientists notice that suggested a single theory could describe every gas?

choices.text: All gases share certain physical behaviors.
All gases are made of the same kind of particle.
choices.why: Different gases are different substances made of different particles. It was their shared physical behavior, not a shared makeup, that pointed to one theory.

choices.text: All gases have the same chemical properties.
choices.why: Gases differ chemically; hydrogen burns in air, for example. What gases have in common are certain physical behaviors.

choices.text: All gases are lighter than air.
choices.why: Hydrogen and helium are lighter than air, but air is itself a gas, so this can't be true of every gas. The common ground was physical behavior, not density.

explanation: It did not take long to recognize that all gases share certain physical behaviors, which suggested that one all-encompassing theory could describe them. Today that theory is the kinetic theory of gases.

prompt: The kinetic theory of gases is called a theory. In science, what does calling it a theory indicate?

choices.text: It explains many observations of gases and is backed by much evidence.
It is only a guess about gases that scientists have not yet tested.
choices.why: That is the everyday meaning of "theory." In science, a theory explains a large number of observations and is backed by a great deal of evidence.

choices.text: It is a statement about gases that is never violated in any way.
choices.why: That describes a scientific law. Real gases deviate slightly from the kinetic theory, so it is not thought to be inviolate.

choices.text: It describes how one particular gas behaves, not gases in general.
choices.why: The kinetic theory is meant to be one all-encompassing theory that describes all gases, not just one.

explanation: In science, a theory is a general statement that explains a large number of observations, and calling something a theory signals that there is a great deal of evidence for it. The kinetic theory explains many observations of how gases behave.

prompt: A student says that air is "nothing" because it is invisible. Which statement of the kinetic theory shows that the student is wrong?

choices.text: Gases consist of tiny particles of matter.
Gas particles are tiny compared with the distances between them.
choices.why: This is part of the theory, but it describes how the particles are spaced, not whether a gas is made of matter.

choices.text: Collisions between gas particles are elastic.
choices.why: This describes what happens to energy when particles collide, not whether a gas is made of matter.

choices.text: The average speed of gas particles depends on temperature.
choices.why: This links the particles' speed to temperature; it doesn't address whether a gas is made of matter.

explanation: The first statement of the kinetic theory is that gases consist of tiny particles of matter in constant motion. Air is made of such particles; they are simply far too small to see one by one.

prompt: According to the kinetic theory, which description fits the motion of one particle in a sample of gas held in a closed container?

choices.text: It keeps moving, changing direction when it hits particles or walls.
It travels in one straight line forever without hitting anything.
choices.why: Gas particles are constantly colliding with each other and with the walls of the container, so a particle's path keeps changing.

choices.text: It sits still until another particle strikes it and sets it moving.
choices.why: Gas particles are in constant motion; they are never at rest waiting to be hit.

choices.text: It sticks to the container wall the first time it hits it.
choices.why: Gas particles are in constant motion; a particle bounces off the wall and keeps moving rather than stopping there.

explanation: The kinetic theory says gas particles are in constant motion and are constantly colliding with each other and with the walls of their container. Each particle keeps moving and keeps changing direction.

prompt: The kinetic theory states that the collisions between gas particles are elastic. What does elastic mean in this statement?

choices.text: There is no net loss of energy from the collisions.
The particles stretch and change shape when they collide.
choices.why: In everyday speech, elastic means stretchy, but here it describes energy: the collisions cause no net loss of energy.

choices.text: The particles stick together for a moment after they collide.
choices.why: Elastic describes what happens to energy in a collision, not sticking. Colliding gas particles bounce apart and stay in constant motion.

choices.text: The particles lose a small amount of energy in every collision.
choices.why: That is the opposite of an elastic collision, which has no net loss of energy.

explanation: An elastic collision is one with no net loss of energy. However often gas particles collide with each other and with the walls, they lose no energy overall.

prompt: Suppose the collisions between the particles of a gas in a sealed container were not elastic, and no heat were added to the gas. What would happen to the gas over time?

choices.text: Its particles would gradually slow down, and the gas would get colder.
Its particles would gradually speed up, and the gas would get hotter.
choices.why: Collisions that are not elastic lose energy; they don't add it. Losing energy of motion slows the particles and lowers the temperature.

choices.text: Nothing would change, because only temperature controls particle speed.
choices.why: Temperature is a measure of the particles' average energy of motion, so if collisions drained that energy, the temperature itself would fall.

choices.text: Its particles would begin to attract one another strongly.
choices.why: Whether collisions are elastic concerns energy, not forces between particles. Losing energy would slow the particles down.

explanation: Elastic collisions cause no net loss of energy. If the collisions did lose energy, the particles would slow down on average, and because temperature measures the average energy of motion, the gas would cool.

prompt: According to the kinetic theory, what is found in the space between the particles of a gas?

choices.text: Empty space, with nothing in it
Air that fills the gaps between them
choices.why: Air is itself a gas made of particles. Between the particles of any gas, air included, there is only empty space.

choices.text: Heat that pushes the particles apart
choices.why: Heat is not a substance that fills the gaps. Temperature is related to how fast the particles move; the space between them is empty.

choices.text: Smaller particles of the same gas
choices.why: The theory pictures a gas as tiny particles separated by large distances, and those distances are empty, not packed with more particles.

explanation: Gas particles are tiny compared with the large distances that separate them, and those distances are empty space. Most of a gas is empty space.

prompt: A flask is filled with 1.0 L of a gas. If all of the gas particles could be packed tightly together, with no space between them, about how much volume would the particles themselves take up?

choices.text: A tiny part of the 1.0 L
About half of the 1.0 L
choices.why: That would make the particles about as large as the spaces between them. The kinetic theory says gas particles are tiny compared with the distances that separate them.

choices.text: Nearly all of the 1.0 L
choices.why: The particles move throughout the flask, but they take up very little of it; most of the volume is empty space.

choices.text: Somewhat more than 1.0 L
choices.why: Packing the particles together can't make them take up more room than the gas did, and most of that room was empty space to begin with.

explanation: Gas particles are tiny compared with the distances that separate them, so most of a gas is empty space. Packed together, the particles would fill only a very small part of the flask.

prompt: You seal the tip of a syringe full of air and push on the plunger. The plunger moves in, squeezing the air into a smaller volume. Which statement of the kinetic theory best explains why the air can be compressed this way?

choices.text: Gas particles are tiny compared with the distances between them.
Gas particles are in constant motion.
choices.why: Motion alone doesn't make room for compression. What allows it is the large amount of empty space between the particles.

choices.text: Collisions between gas particles are elastic.
choices.why: Elastic collisions concern energy, not space. The air can be compressed because most of it is empty space between particles.

choices.text: The average speed of gas particles depends on temperature.
choices.why: This links particle speed to temperature; it says nothing about the room between particles that lets a gas be compressed.

explanation: Because gas particles are separated by large distances, most of a gas is empty space. Pushing the plunger simply moves the particles closer together, which is why a gas can contract.

prompt: A sample of gas is squeezed into a smaller volume without changing its temperature. According to the kinetic theory, what has changed about its particles?

choices.text: They are closer together, but each particle is the same size as before.
Each particle has shrunk, so the particles fit into less space.
choices.why: The particles themselves don't shrink. Compression only reduces the large empty spaces between them.

choices.text: They have stopped moving and are packed against one another.
choices.why: Gas particles are in constant motion, and the compressed gas is still a gas; its particles are closer together but still separated by empty space.

choices.text: Some particles have been destroyed, so fewer of them remain.
choices.why: Squeezing a gas doesn't destroy any particles; the same particles simply occupy a smaller space.

explanation: Most of a gas is empty space, so compressing it just reduces the distances between the particles. The particles themselves, and the number of them, stay the same.

prompt: Steam has a much lower density than liquid water, even though both are made of H2O molecules. Which explanation agrees with the kinetic theory?

choices.text: In steam, the H2O molecules are spread far apart from one another.
Each H2O molecule in steam has less mass than one in liquid water.
choices.why: An H2O molecule has the same mass whether it is in steam or in liquid water. The difference is how far apart the molecules are.

choices.text: Each H2O molecule in steam is smaller than one in liquid water.
choices.why: Changing from liquid to gas doesn't change the size of the molecules; the low density comes from the large distances between them.

choices.text: In steam, the H2O molecules have broken apart into H and O atoms.
choices.why: Boiling water is a physical change, so steam is still made of H2O molecules, just much farther apart.

explanation: Gas particles are separated by large distances compared with their size, so most of a gas is empty space. A given volume of steam holds far fewer H2O molecules, and far less mass, than the same volume of liquid water.

prompt: A student claims that gas particles push one another away whenever they come close together. How does this claim compare with the kinetic theory?

choices.text: It disagrees: the theory says gas particles neither attract nor repel one another.
It agrees: repulsion is what makes the collisions between gas particles elastic.
choices.why: Elastic describes the energy in a collision, not a force between particles. The theory says there are no forces between gas particles.

choices.text: It disagrees: the theory says gas particles attract one another instead.
choices.why: The theory rules out attraction as well as repulsion: there are no interactive forces between gas particles.

choices.text: It agrees: the theory says gas particles repel but never attract one another.
choices.why: The theory rules out both kinds of force. Gas particles neither attract nor repel one another.

explanation: One statement of the kinetic theory is that there are no interactive forces, neither attraction nor repulsion, between the particles of a gas. The student's claim contradicts it.

prompt: A small amount of gas is released at one end of a large container from which all the air has been removed. According to the kinetic theory, where will the gas particles be shortly afterward?

choices.text: Spread out through the whole container, still moving
Still clustered near the end where they were released
choices.why: There are no attractive forces holding gas particles together, and they are in constant motion, so they move out into the empty space.

choices.text: Collected at the bottom of the container, like a liquid
choices.why: Gas particles are in constant motion, so they don't settle into a pile at the bottom the way a liquid does.

choices.text: Spread partway, then stopped once they had slowed down
choices.why: Gas particles don't run down and stop. Their collisions are elastic, so they stay in constant motion.

explanation: Gas particles are in constant motion, and no attractive forces hold them together, so they move into all of the space available to them.

prompt: A dense gas fills the bottom half of a closed container, and a much less dense gas fills the top half. Nothing is stirred, and the temperature stays constant. What does the kinetic theory predict?

choices.text: The gases mix evenly, because their particles are in constant motion.
The gases stay in two layers, like oil floating on water.
choices.why: Gas particles never stop moving, so the particles of each gas travel into the other. Two or more gases will always mix.

choices.text: The gases mix only where they touch, leaving most of each unmixed.
choices.why: The particles keep moving throughout the container, so mixing doesn't stop at the boundary; the gases end up mixed evenly.

choices.text: The gases mix for a while and then separate back into layers.
choices.why: The particles keep moving and colliding throughout the container, so once the gases are mixed, they stay mixed.

explanation: Because gas particles are in constant motion, the particles of each gas move and collide throughout the container. Two or more gases will always mix, even when one is much denser than the other.

prompt: A sealed flask of gas is cooled from 50 °C to 0 °C, and the substance remains a gas. According to the kinetic theory, what happens to its particles?

choices.text: They move more slowly on average but stay in constant motion.
They stop moving completely once the gas reaches 0 °C.
choices.why: Gas particles are in constant motion at any temperature. 0 °C is the freezing point of water, not a temperature at which particles stop.

choices.text: They move faster on average to keep the gas from cooling.
choices.why: Temperature is a measure of the particles' average energy of motion, so a lower temperature means a lower average speed.

choices.text: They keep exactly the same average speed they had at 50 °C.
choices.why: The average speed of gas particles depends on the temperature of the gas, so cooling the gas lowers it.

explanation: The average speed of gas particles depends on temperature, and a lower temperature means less energy of motion, so the particles slow down. They never stop, though: gas particles are in constant motion.

prompt: Two identical sealed flasks hold equal amounts of the same gas. One flask is at 20 °C and the other is at 80 °C. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: The particles in the 80 °C flask have the greater average speed.
The particles in both flasks have the same average speed.
choices.why: The average speed of gas particles depends on temperature, so the same gas at two different temperatures has two different average speeds.

choices.text: The particles in the 20 °C flask have the greater average speed.
choices.why: Temperature measures the average energy of motion of the particles, so the hotter gas has the faster particles.

choices.text: The particles in the 80 °C flask are larger than those at 20 °C.
choices.why: Heating a gas changes how fast its particles move, not how big they are.

explanation: The average speed of gas particles depends on temperature. Since temperature is a measure of the average energy of motion, the particles at 80 °C move faster on average than those at 20 °C.

prompt: The same gas, at the same temperature, fills a small flask and a large tank. How does the average speed of the gas particles in the flask compare with that in the tank?

choices.text: It is the same, because the gas is at the same temperature in both.
It is lower in the flask, because the particles have less room to move.
choices.why: The kinetic theory ties the average speed of gas particles to temperature, not to the size of the container.

choices.text: It is higher in the flask, because the particles are closer together.
choices.why: Being closer together doesn't change the particles' average speed; that depends on temperature, which is the same in both containers.

choices.text: It is higher in the tank, because the tank holds more particles.
choices.why: The number of particles doesn't set their average speed. At the same temperature, the average speed is the same.

explanation: The kinetic theory states that the average speed of gas particles depends on the temperature of the gas. The flask and the tank hold the same gas at the same temperature, so the average speeds are the same.

prompt: The same amount of air freshener is sprayed into one corner of each of two identical closed rooms with still air. One room is at 15 °C and the other is at 30 °C. In which room should the scent reach the far corner sooner, and why?

choices.text: The 30 °C room, because the gas particles there move faster on average.
The 15 °C room, because the colder air is denser and carries the scent.
choices.why: Gases mix because their particles move, and the particles move faster on average at a higher temperature, so the scent spreads faster in the warmer room.

choices.text: Both rooms equally, because gases always mix at the same rate.
choices.why: Gases always mix, but the mixing comes from the particles' motion, and they move faster on average at a higher temperature.

choices.text: The 30 °C room, because the scent particles grow larger and fill more space.
choices.why: The warmer room is right, but not for that reason: heating speeds up the particles; it doesn't make them larger.

explanation: Gases mix because their particles are in constant motion, and the average speed of the particles depends on temperature. In the warmer room the particles move faster on average, so the scent spreads across the room sooner.

prompt: What is an ideal gas?

choices.text: A gas that exactly follows every statement of the kinetic theory
The gas best suited to a job, such as helium for a balloon
choices.why: In chemistry, "ideal" has a specific meaning: an ideal gas is one that follows the statements of the kinetic theory exactly.

choices.text: Any gas whose particles are in constant motion
choices.why: Constant motion is only one statement of the kinetic theory. An ideal gas follows all of the statements exactly.

choices.text: A gas made of only one element, such as He or O2
choices.why: Whether a gas is ideal depends on how it behaves, not on how many elements it contains.

explanation: An ideal gas is defined by its behavior: it is a gas that exactly follows the statements of the kinetic theory of gases, every one of them.

prompt: Real gases are not ideal gases. Why, then, is the kinetic theory of gases well accepted by the scientific community?

choices.text: Most gases deviate only slightly from it, so it describes them well.
Real gases behave exactly like ideal gases once they are heated.
choices.why: Real gases are not ideal, and heating doesn't make a real gas follow the theory exactly. The theory is accepted because most gases deviate only slightly.

choices.text: The theory is very old, and old theories are rarely questioned.
choices.why: A theory is accepted because of the evidence supporting it, not because of its age. Most gases follow this one closely.

choices.text: Scientists use only ideal gases when they do experiments.
choices.why: An ideal gas is a model; every gas used in an experiment is a real gas. The theory works because real gases deviate only slightly from it.

explanation: Real gases deviate slightly from perfect agreement with the kinetic theory, but most gases follow its statements closely. Because the theory describes the behavior of gases so well, it is well accepted.

prompt: Which of these imaginary gases could be an ideal gas?

choices.text: Its particles are tiny and far apart, and they never stop moving.
Its particles lose a little energy each time they collide.
choices.why: An ideal gas has elastic collisions with no net loss of energy, so this gas breaks one of the statements of the kinetic theory.

choices.text: Its particles take up about half of the container's volume.
choices.why: In an ideal gas, the particles are tiny compared with the distances between them, so they fill only a tiny part of the container.

choices.text: Its particles slowly settle and come to rest on the bottom.
choices.why: The particles of an ideal gas are in constant motion; they never come to rest.

explanation: An ideal gas must follow every statement of the kinetic theory exactly. Tiny, widely separated particles in constant motion fit those statements; each of the other gases breaks one of them.

prompt: Careful measurements show that the particles of a certain gas attract one another slightly. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.text: It is not ideal, because it breaks the theory's statement about forces.
It is still ideal, because the attraction between its particles is slight.
choices.why: An ideal gas follows every statement of the kinetic theory exactly, so even a slight attraction means this gas is not ideal.

choices.text: It cannot be a gas, because gas particles never attract one another.
choices.why: Real gases deviate slightly from the kinetic theory and are still gases. This one is simply not ideal.

choices.text: It is not ideal, because its collisions with one another cannot be elastic.
choices.why: Attraction between particles concerns the statement about forces, not the statement about energy in collisions.

explanation: An ideal gas follows every statement of the kinetic theory exactly, including the one about forces between particles. A gas whose particles attract one another is a real gas that deviates from the theory, but it is still a gas.
